cells.tense: Right now you're tending what's alive and seeing what it needs next.
cells.ask: Ask one living thing what it needs today, then do that one thing and stop.
cells.core:
You're with what you're growing — not forcing it, not looking past it. You can picture how it might turn out without insisting it go there. And you keep your hands soft while you wait, which is harder than it sounds.

That quiet imagining and the care you're giving are running at the same time. You sense something opening before it shows, and you let it open on its own schedule. What you're feeding here, you're feeding on purpose. Wonder and care aren't two jobs you're juggling — they're the same attention, and right now it's steady.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what's growing and see what's next without forcing it.
cells.verb: imagining what hasn't happened yet, with a beginner's wonder
cells.place: at the edge of something that is still growing

cells.tense: You're already out there, braced at a future that hasn't arrived and can't be written in yet.
cells.ask: Pick one growing thing and leave it alone for a day, just watching what it does without your hand.
cells.core:
You care so much that you're ahead of what you're growing. You picture every branch, every thing that could go wrong, and you step in before it's asked. Some of what you're holding is a shape you handed yourself.

Read the signs early and get ready — that's the health of this, and it looks like steady hands. Right now the cost is the thing in front of you, and careful care has slid into a job you can't put down. You're spending tomorrow's attention on today's sprout. One thing you're growing can go a day without your hand on it.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying what hasn't happened yet, and it's wearing you thin.
cells.verb: imagining what hasn't happened yet, with a beginner's wonder

cells.tense: You kept watch over what was growing, and back then you kept your own seeing out of it.
cells.ask: Tell one person something you find beautiful about what you're growing, without fixing anything after.
cells.core:
You gave what you were growing the guarded kind of care. You kept watch, but you didn't dream it forward — no picture of how it might turn out, no letting yourself feel what it could become.

Effort isn't the lack here. Imagining is. You've gone quiet in the one place where care comes alive, and you've been treating that quiet as if it were the whole of you. It isn't. Start small: let one real thing you're growing be beautiful to you, and say so out loud where someone can hear it. That's not the same as feeding it. It's remembering why you ever wanted to.
cells.sheetLine: You kept watch, but you stopped dreaming what you tend forward.

cells.tense: You're already imagining what hasn't happened yet, and you call it something else.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're quietly hoping for in what you tend, then let yourself do one small thing about it.
cells.core:
When you picture how something you're tending might turn out, that's imagining ahead — you just call it planning, or notice, or being practical. The wonder is working, and you haven't said so.

Care with an eye on what's coming is the shape this takes when it's healthy: you feel the depth in what's growing and move on its behalf, no push and no clinging. The picture is yours, and you keep it on the shelf where it belongs to circumstance. So say one small hope out loud, to yourself or someone else, then do the next practical thing that serves it. Owning what you already see.
cells.sheetLine: You're already imagining what's next. You just haven't claimed it.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that care has stopped meaning keeping watch or imagining ahead. A reader could say they are still very much present in what they tend, just tired. If wrong, the ask — ask what the sprout needs today — is still usable, because it makes attention land on one living thing in its actual timing. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'You know what it needs before it does.'
